qualityBar.verdict: Locomotion clears the PlayBound Bar as the affordable, DRM-free foundation for a deep transport sandbox and its modern OpenLoco edition.

expected.longDescription:
Chris Sawyer’s Locomotion hands you a landscape, a century of transport technology, and the dangerous idea that every town can be connected. Railways are the star, but buses, trucks, trams, aircraft, and ships all compete for space and attention.

The pleasure is in building systems that begin as sketches and become indispensable. A short coal line funds a passenger network. A crowded station demands longer trains. New industries appear, cities spread toward your routes, and an improvised junction becomes the beating heart of an empire.

This catalog entry is the commercial master copy. Its graphics, music, sounds, scenarios, and object data are required by OpenLoco, the modern open-source reimplementation PlayBound recommends for everyday play. Buying the DRM-free GOG release provides those assets without requiring GOG Galaxy after download.

The original executable remains a capable single-player strategy game, but current Windows compatibility can be uneven and its advertised multiplayer is not available in the current GOG package. PlayBound therefore keeps multiplayer, servers, controllers, and party features off this master record. OpenLoco is also currently single-player; its developers have prepared internal architecture for possible multiplayer, but that is not a shipped feature.

Treat this page as ownership made clear. Purchase and download the offline installer once, let PlayBound locate the installed data, then use the OpenLoco edition for modern displays, portability, active fixes, and a cleaner launch. The base game is the ticket; the edition is the comfortable seat.
expected.whyWePickedIt: We added Locomotion as a master copy because OpenLoco legally and technically depends on its commercial asset files. The GOG release is inexpensive, DRM-free, and does not require Galaxy once downloaded. Keeping ownership on the base record lets the OpenLoco edition remain an honest direct one-click engine install without pretending the original art and audio are freely redistributable.
expected.thatOneThing: Every route becomes a living machine

installSteps.text: Purchase Chris Sawyer’s Locomotion from GOG. This master copy supplies the commercial graphics, audio, scenarios, and object data.
Download the DRM-free offline installer from your GOG library. Galaxy is optional and is not required for PlayBound’s setup.
Install once or point PlayBound at an existing Locomotion folder. The launcher verifies the required data without uploading or redistributing it.
Choose the OpenLoco edition in PlayBound. The modern engine installs separately and reads the legally owned data from the managed base-game folder.

qualityBar.verdict: A transport sandbox where the most satisfying sight is a junction you no longer need to babysit.

set.longDescription:
Chris Sawyer's Locomotion gives you a map full of towns, industries and opportunities to create traffic. Build a short rail line to move coal, then add buses to serve the growing town, then notice the coal train is blocking every passenger service you just made profitable. The game turns a transport diagram into a living set of deadlines and bottlenecks. When a route finally works without intervention, the relief is as good as the money it earns.

There are more than 40 scenarios, and the timeline carries you from the age of early rail through newer vehicles. Trains are the headline, but road vehicles, trams, ships and aircraft expand the ways you can connect people and goods. Rival companies compete for the same opportunities. The detailed maps reward close attention: a track layout that looked tidy at first can become a problem when two services need the same junction. You do not need a scripted story to create a memorable disaster; a town growing faster than your network can manage is plenty.

The interface carries its 2004 age openly. Building complex routes asks for repeated clicks, and some tools feel slower than their modern equivalents. The official GOG copy is Windows only and DRM-free, so an owner can download an offline installer without running Galaxy. GOG explicitly says multiplayer is unavailable in its current release. Steam's storefront lists a multiplayer feature, but that label alone does not establish a working PlayBound party flow for the GOG package. We are keeping the base listing single-player until a specific supported build and connection path are tested. It has no documented native gamepad support; a mouse remains the sensible way to lay track and manage windows.

This commercial copy also matters to OpenLoco. The open-source reimplementation can modernize the engine, but it still needs the original Locomotion assets that players legally own. Buying the GOG version and letting PlayBound locate the installed game keeps that dependency honest. OpenLoco is a separate edition, not a reason to describe the base game as free or actively maintained. We do not copy a synthetic 1080p/60fps recommendation into the hardware section: GOG publishes only a 1.8 GHz CPU, 512 MB RAM, DirectX 7-era graphics and 2 GB of storage, alongside an unusually specific old AMD/ATI driver warning.

Locomotion is for people who enjoy watching a plan collide with the details of a working network. The first profitable route is pleasant; the tenth route sharing its station is where the game starts to bite. It is old-fashioned, sometimes awkward, and still capable of making a small train line feel like a personal engineering triumph.
set.whyWePickedIt: Locomotion remains a strong transport sandbox, and the DRM-free GOG copy gives OpenLoco owners the original assets it legally requires. We like the way a simple route grows into a whole network of competing schedules. Its aging interface and unavailable GOG multiplayer deserve the same clear treatment as its strengths.
set.thatOneThing: You build one harmless coal line, then spend the next three hours untangling a station that has become the national rail crisis.
